title: Mental Subtraction for Grade 2: 5 Tricks to Do It in Your Head + Free Quiz
meta_title: Mental Subtraction Grade 2: 5 Head Tricks + Quiz
meta_desc: Teach mental subtraction to your Grade 2 child with five no-paper tricks, from counting up to subtracting 9. Free 8-question quiz and printable practice.
excerpt: No paper, no borrowing, no tears. These are the five mental subtraction tricks I teach Grade 2 children so they can work out 34 − 9 in their head, plus a quick quiz to test them.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Ask a Grade 2 child to work out 34 − 9 and watch what happens. Most reach for a pencil, line the numbers up, and start crossing out tens. But 34 − 9 is a five-second job in your head — if you know the right trick. Mental subtraction for Grade 2 is not about doing sums faster on paper; it is about not needing the paper at all for the everyday ones. That skill pays off every single day, at the shop, on the bus, counting change.

Here are the five head-only strategies I lean on with seven-year-olds, roughly in the order they should meet them. No worksheets required to learn them — just talk them through out loud, with real numbers, while you are doing ordinary things. The written borrowing method has its place, but it is a separate skill for a separate day. Today we stay in the head.

1. Count up to find the difference (the shopkeeper’s way)

This is the one I teach first because children already do it without knowing the name. To find 23 − 18, do not count backwards. Start at 18 and count up to 23: nineteen, twenty, twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three — that is five hops, so the answer is 5. Any Tier-2 city shopkeeper handing back change does exactly this: you give ₹20 for an ₹18 item and he counts ‘eighteen, nineteen, twenty’ into your hand. Two rupees back.

Counting up shines when the two numbers are close together. For 41 − 38 the answer jumps out in three little hops. Subtracting backwards there would be slow and error-prone.

2. Subtract the tens, then the ones

Break the number you are taking away into its tens and its ones, then remove them in two easy steps. For 56 − 23, first take away the 20 (56 becomes 36), then take away the 3 (36 becomes 33). Two small moves instead of one scary one. This splitting is the heart of mental subtraction for Grade 2, and it works beautifully as long as the ones do not cross a ten.

When the ones would cross a ten

For 52 − 27, taking the 20 gives 32, but then 32 − 7 crosses back over thirty. That is fine — a child who knows their number bonds handles it, and it is a nudge toward the count-up method or the round-and-adjust trick below. I would not force splitting on every sum; part of the skill is picking the right tool.

3. Subtract 9 as −10 then +1

Subtracting 9 is fiddly. Subtracting 10 is a joy — you just drop the tens digit by one. So teach the swap: to subtract 9, take away 10 and give 1 back. For 34 − 9, do 34 − 10 = 24, then add 1 to get 25. The same idea handles subtracting 8 (take 10, give 2 back) and subtracting 19 (take 20, give 1 back). Children find this almost like a magic trick once they see it, and it is far kinder than counting back nine times.

4. Use number bonds and the add-subtract inverse

Every subtraction hides an addition. If a child knows the bond 6 + 4 = 10, they already know 10 − 6 = 4 and 10 − 4 = 6 — same picture, read a different way. So when a child stalls on 15 − 8, I ask the flipped question: ‘8 plus what makes 15?’ Suddenly it is friendly. Solid bonds to 10 and 20 are the single biggest thing that makes mental subtraction feel effortless, which is why I drill them more than anything else.

  • Bonds to 10: 1 and 9, 2 and 8, 3 and 7, 4 and 6, 5 and 5.
  • Read each bond four ways — 3 + 7, 7 + 3, 10 − 3, 10 − 7.
  • Check any subtraction by adding back: 13 − 5 = 8, and 8 + 5 = 13, so it is right.

5. Round, subtract, then adjust

For a number ending in 8 or 9, round it up to the nearest ten, subtract that, then give back the little bit. To do 63 − 28, round 28 up to 30: 63 − 30 = 33, then add back 2 to get 35. It is the same thinking as the subtract-9 trick, stretched to bigger numbers. This one asks a bit more of a Grade 2 child, so save it for the second half of the year once the first four are secure.

A realistic way to practise mental subtraction for Grade 2

Ten minutes of out-loud practice beats a page of sums. Turn shopping into a game: ‘This costs ₹27, I am paying ₹50, how much change?’ Ask on the walk to school, no paper allowed. The one honest caveat: do not chase speed too early. A child who reasons out 41 − 38 in four seconds, and can say why, is far stronger than one who has memorised it and cannot explain. The explaining is where real fluency lives.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a short, free quiz built around exactly these tricks — counting up, splitting tens and ones, subtracting 9, and the add-subtract inverse. Let your child answer in their head first, then read each explanation together. When they are ready for longer graded practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives plenty of head-maths questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 2 Mental Subtraction Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on counting up, splitting tens and ones, subtracting 9, and number bonds. Answer each in your head, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: Start at 18 and hop up: 19, 20, 21, 22, 23. That is 5 hops, so the answer is 5.
Take away the tens then the ones: 56 − 20 = 36, then 36 − 3 = 33.

questions.q: 8 plus what makes 15? Use it to find 15 − 8.
questions.explanation: 8 + 7 = 15, so 15 − 8 = 7. Every subtraction hides an addition.
Round 28 up to 30: 63 − 30 = 33, then add back 2 to get 35.

questions.q: Which is the easy way to work out 47 − 9?
questions.explanation: Subtracting 9 is the same as subtracting 10 and giving 1 back: 47 − 10 = 37, then 37 + 1 = 38.
The numbers are close, so count up from 38: 39, 40, 41. That is 3 hops, so the answer is 3.

questions.q: A toy costs ₹27. You pay ₹30. How much change?
questions.explanation: Count up from 27 to 30: 28, 29, 30. That is 3, so the change is ₹3.

faq.q: What is mental subtraction and why teach it in Grade 2?
faq.a: It means working out a subtraction in your head without writing it down. Grade 2 is the right time because the numbers are small enough to hold in mind, and the head tricks — counting up, subtracting 9 as −10 then +1 — build real number sense that speeds up everything later.

faq.q: Should my child learn mental subtraction or the written borrowing method first?
faq.a: Mental tricks first, for the everyday sums. The written borrowing method is for larger or trickier numbers and is a separate skill. A child who can already do 34 − 9 in their head understands borrowing far more easily when it comes.

faq.q: My child gets stuck subtracting across a ten. What helps?
faq.a: Flip it into an addition. For 15 − 8, ask ‘8 plus what makes 15?’ instead. Strong number bonds to 10 and 20 fix most of these stalls, so drill the bonds until they are instant.

faq.q: How much daily practice does mental subtraction need?
faq.a: About ten minutes of out-loud practice, ideally woven into real life like shopping and change. Little and often beats a long weekly session. Ask the questions during ordinary moments and keep paper out of it.
